summaries.example: Imagine an architect planning a house. Before the house is built, the plan exists in the architect’s mind. Norris thought nature is like that: the things in the world follow patterns or ideas that exist in God’s mind. He called this hidden pattern-world the intelligible world.
summaries.summary: John Norris was an English philosopher and Christian writer who wanted to explain how God, ideas, nature, and human knowledge fit together. He was strongly influenced by René Descartes and Nicolas Malebranche, while also using ideas from Plato and earlier Christian and Scholastic thinkers. Norris argued that the natural world has an ideal pattern in God’s mind. He called this pattern-world the intelligible world. In his view, people know things through ideas connected with God, not simply through their senses. He also defended the difference between mind and body and argued that the soul is not a material body. Norris thought God is simple, meaning that God’s qualities are not separate pieces. They are different ways people understand the same divine reality. He believed careful thinking and calm meditation could help people seek truth and live well, while also admitting that human knowledge of God is incomplete.
key_ideas: Norris thought God’s mind contains the patterns or ideas that guide the created world.
He believed eternal truths, such as truths about perfect shapes, depend on God and are not changed by human opinions.
He followed Descartes in saying that mind and body are really different kinds of things.
He believed human thinking can give us knowledge, but our understanding of God is still partial.
summaries.why_it_matters: Norris helps us see how philosophers once debated big questions about minds, bodies, truth, and God. His arguments also show why people can disagree about where knowledge begins: with reason and clear thinking, or with experience through the senses. Studying him helps us understand how one thinker combined philosophy with religious beliefs.

important_terms.definition: A seventeenth-century English philosopher who connected ideas from Descartes, Malebranche, Plato, and Christian theology.
A realm of patterns and ideas that Norris said exists in God’s mind and helps explain the natural world.
The view that God is not made of separate parts. God’s different qualities are ways humans think about one divine reality.
A way of thinking carefully about something by considering one feature without the other features that usually come with it.

questions_to_think_about: Could a perfect circle exist in nature, or only as an idea?
Does being able to imagine a mind without a body prove they are separate?
Can people know some truths even when they do not understand everything about God?

summaries.example: Suppose someone reasons about a perfect triangle. No physical drawing is perfectly exact, yet geometry studies necessary truths about triangles. Norris would argue that such truths cannot be based only on changing physical objects. They depend on ideal structures, which he located in the divine mind. A critic might instead ask whether our ideas guarantee anything beyond our own thinking. That disagreement points toward the larger rationalist-empiricist debate.
summaries.summary: John Norris was a late-seventeenth-century English philosopher whose work continued the Cartesian project while responding to the growing influence of Locke’s empiricism. His central ambition was to develop Malebranche’s account of the intelligible world. Norris argued that creation requires an ideal counterpart to nature: God must possess the patterns or essential reasons according to which creatures are made. He supported this conclusion through several lines of argument, including the existence of natural kinds, our grasp of perfect geometrical objects, the possibility of eternal truths, and the necessary objects of demonstrative sciences. These divine ideas are located in God and are really identical with the divine essence. Norris therefore had to explain how God can contain ideas such as extension without becoming material. His answer uses eminent containment: God contains created perfections in a higher, intellectual manner rather than formally possessing them as physical properties. This account is tied to divine simplicity. God’s attributes and ideas are one in reality, although human minds distinguish them according to different objects and operations. Norris also held that all thought has a formal aspect, the act of thinking, and an objective aspect, what is thought about. Following Malebranche, he claimed that the ultimate object is God as expressed through divine ideas. Following Descartes, he defended the real distinction between mind and body and rejected Locke’s suggestion that matter might think. The entry also identifies a tension in this defense: if the soul’s essence is not available to us, it may be difficult to use that essence in a proof. key_ideas: Norris aimed to extend and complete Malebranche’s account of the intelligible world by arguing for divine ideas as the grounds of nature, truth, universals, and scientific knowledge.
His arguments appeal to creation, natural kinds, perfect geometrical objects, the possibility of eternal truth, the existence of demonstrative sciences, and the existence of God.
He maintained that divine ideas are identical with God’s essence, while human beings distinguish divine attributes only in their manner of conceiving them.
Norris adopted a Cartesian account of thought but a Malebranchean account of its content: thought has an act or structure, while its object is always God understood through divine ideas.

He reconstructed the real-distinction argument to oppose Locke’s possibility that matter might think, though the entry notes a difficulty: Norris also says we lack direct access to the essence of the soul.

Norris treated reason as reliable but limited. He opposed both reducing religious truth to what humans can fully comprehend and replacing ordinary understanding with a special, extraordinary inner inspiration.
summaries.why_it_matters: Norris is important because his arguments make the late-seventeenth-century conflict between rationalism and empiricism especially clear. He shows how claims about ideas lead to claims about reality, God, the soul, and scientific knowledge. His work also illustrates a recurring philosophical problem: a theory may try to explain divine simplicity, human certainty, and the contents of thought at once, yet the connections among those parts can create new difficulties. Reading Norris therefore helps students examine not only conclusions but also the assumptions that make an argument possible.

important_terms.definition: Norris’s name for the realm of divine ideas that provides the patterns, objects, or grounds of human knowledge.
The position that God’s ideas are really identical with the divine essence, even though humans distinguish them in thought.
A relation in which an effect exists in its cause in a higher or more intellectual way, as a building exists as a plan in an architect’s mind.
The process of considering one aspect of something without treating that aspect as an independently existing substance.
The Cartesian claim that mind and body are two genuinely different substances rather than merely two features of one substance.
The claim that matter might have thought added to it, a possibility associated in the entry with Locke’s debate about mind and body.
The view that perception, including sensory and intellectual perception, is perception of ideas in God.
The philosophical position that emphasizes reason and necessary knowledge; the entry places Norris firmly in this camp in contrast with empiricism.

questions_to_think_about: If a person can clearly conceive of mind without body, does that establish a real distinction, or only a difference in concepts?
Can eternal truths be explained without placing them in a divine mind?
Does saying that divine attributes are really one but distinct in human thought solve, or merely restate, the problem of divine simplicity?
If our ideas are grounded in God, what role remains for sensory experience in knowledge?
Is human ignorance a reason to reject a claim, or can something be true even when it is incomprehensible to us?

summaries.example: Think about a map of a new city. The map is not the city, but it gives a planned pattern for finding streets and buildings. Norris thought the natural world is similar to a pattern held in God’s mind. He believed that when we understand nature or geometry, we are reaching toward these deeper ideas. Someone influenced by Locke might reply that our ideas begin with what we see and experience, so a map-like pattern in God’s mind has not been proved.
summaries.summary: John Norris was an English philosopher who wrote about God, knowledge, the soul, religion, and human life. He was influenced by Descartes, Malebranche, Plato, Augustine, Aquinas, and Scholastic philosophy. His main project was to improve Malebranche’s explanation of the intelligible world, which Norris understood as the realm of ideas in God’s mind. Norris argued that nature must have ideal patterns. A created thing cannot be the complete source of its own existence, and the order of nature suggests that creation follows ideas already present in God. He also appealed to our thoughts of perfect circles and other geometrical objects. Since physical examples are never perfectly exact, Norris believed that such knowledge points to ideal objects. He connected these ideas with eternal truths and with sciences that study universal and necessary matters. Norris also developed an account of divine simplicity. God is not made of separate parts or qualities. God’s ideas and attributes are really one with the divine essence, although people think of them in different ways. To explain how God can contain an idea of extension without being a physical thing, Norris used eminent containment: a creator can contain a result in a higher, intellectual way, as an architect contains a building in a plan. He followed Malebranche in saying that the deepest object of thought is God through divine ideas. He followed Descartes in defending a real distinction between mind and body and argued against Locke’s possibility that matter might think. key_ideas: Norris tried to develop Malebranche’s account of God and the ideal world.
He argued that the world needs ideal patterns in God’s mind because created things cannot explain their own existence or perfect order.
He thought perfect shapes, eternal truths, and universal sciences point beyond changing physical objects.
He said our thoughts have an act of thinking and an object being thought about; the ultimate object is God’s ideas.
He defended the difference between mind and body, but the entry notes a challenge about whether we know the soul’s essence well enough to prove this difference.
He held that reason matters in religion, while warning that human beings cannot understand every divine mystery.
summaries.why_it_matters: Norris gives us a clear case study in how one philosopher connects several questions: What is real? How do we know it? What is a mind? What is God like? His disagreements with Locke show that debates about knowledge can affect views about the soul and the physical world. His work also teaches that an argument can be creative and influential while still leaving questions for later thinkers.

important_terms.definition: The world of ideal patterns or divine ideas that Norris believed explains nature and makes knowledge possible.
The belief that God is one undivided reality, even though people describe God with many attributes, such as wisdom or power.
A method of thinking about one feature of a thing while temporarily setting aside other features.
Descartes’ claim that mind and body are genuinely different substances, not merely different properties of one thing.
The possibility that a material body could somehow have thought, which Norris argued against in his debate with Locke.
Norris’s view that people perceive divine ideas when they think and, in a broader sense, when they sense.
A philosophical approach that gives reason a central role in finding necessary and certain knowledge.
The view that knowledge should be based mainly on experience and the senses; the entry connects this approach with Locke.

questions_to_think_about: Are perfect geometric shapes found in the world, or do they exist only in thought?
Why might someone think that a pattern in God’s mind is needed to explain nature?
Would clear thinking alone prove that mind and body are different?
Can a person reject a belief just because it is difficult to understand?
Which seems more convincing: Norris’s emphasis on reason or Locke’s emphasis on experience?
